title: Kubernetes Deployment Strategies: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on shipping changes safely to Kubernetes: rolling updates and readiness gating, Helm per-environment values, GitOps with Argo CD or Flux, canary releases, and rollback.

chapters.title: Rolling Updates and Readiness Gating
points: Deployment rolling update (default strategy RollingUpdate): a new ReplicaSet scales up while the old one scales down, so pods are replaced gradually with no full outage
maxSurge: extra pods allowed above desired replicas during rollout (number or %, default 25%, rounded up); maxUnavailable: pods allowed below desired (default 25%, rounded down)
Zero-downtime setup: maxUnavailable: 0 with maxSurge: 1 (new pod must be Ready before an old one is removed); maxSurge: 0 with maxUnavailable: 1 trades capacity for no extra resources
Readiness probe gates the rollout: a new pod counts as available only after it passes readiness, and the rollout stalls if it never does, so old pods keep serving traffic

Gotchas: no readiness probe means pods are Ready at container start and a broken build still rolls out fully; the probe must check real dependencies not just a port; set minReadySeconds and progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600s) so a stuck rollout is marked failed

chapters.title: Helm Charts and Per-Environment Values
points: Helm chart = Chart.yaml + values.yaml + templates/; a release is one installed instance of a chart, with revision history stored in cluster Secrets
Templates render with Go templating using .Values; defaults live in values.yaml and are overridden per environment: helm upgrade --install app ./chart -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=1.4.2

Override precedence, lowest to highest: chart values.yaml, then -f files in order (later wins), then --set; keep one values-<env>.yaml per environment holding only the differences (replicas, resources, ingress host)
Preview and debug before applying: helm template (render locally), helm diff upgrade (plugin), helm lint, helm upgrade --install --atomic --wait (auto-rollback on failure)

Gotchas: secrets committed in values files (use external secrets or sealed secrets); unpinned image tags like latest; copy-pasting whole values files per env so they drift; --set overriding lists replaces the whole list

chapters.title: GitOps with Argo CD and Flux
points: GitOps: Git is the single source of truth for desired cluster state, and an in-cluster controller pulls and reconciles it continuously; no CI job runs kubectl apply against the cluster

Argo CD: an Application CRD points at repo, path, and target revision; sync status (Synced/OutOfSync) and health are shown in a UI; settings syncPolicy.automated with prune: true and selfHeal: true revert manual drift
Flux: composed of GitRepository (source) and Kustomization or HelmRelease (apply) resources, driven by controllers and configured purely through CRDs with no built-in UI
Argo CD vs Flux: Argo CD is app-centric with a UI and multi-cluster management; Flux is lighter, CLI and CRD native, and strong with image-update automation

Gotchas: kubectl edit on a live cluster gets reverted by selfHeal; prune can delete resources removed from Git; CI should only build the image and commit the new tag to the config repo; roll back by git revert, not by kubectl

chapters.title: Canary Releases with Service Mesh or Argo Rollouts
points: Canary: send a small share of traffic (for example 5% then 25%, 50%, 100%) to the new version and promote only if metrics stay healthy; a plain Deployment cannot split by exact percentage because traffic follows pod count

Argo Rollouts: a Rollout CRD replaces Deployment and has strategy.canary.steps such as setWeight: 10, pause: {duration: 5m}, setWeight: 50; kubectl argo rollouts promote, abort and get rollout manage it

Exact traffic weights need a router: a service mesh (Istio VirtualService weights, Linkerd SMI) or an ingress controller such as NGINX canary annotations, which Argo Rollouts drives via trafficRouting

AnalysisTemplate runs queries (Prometheus error rate, latency) during steps and auto-aborts and rolls back on failure; compare with blue-green, which runs two full stacks and flips the Service at once

Gotchas: without a traffic router, weight is approximate and based on replica ratios; canary needs enough traffic for metrics to be meaningful; both versions run together so DB and API changes must be backward compatible

chapters.title: Rollback with kubectl rollout and Deployment Cheat Sheet
points: Watch and inspect: kubectl rollout status deploy/app; kubectl rollout history deploy/app (add --revision=N for detail); kubectl set image deploy/app app=img:v2
Roll back: kubectl rollout undo deploy/app (previous revision) or --to-revision=N; it only re-applies the old pod template, not ConfigMap or Secret changes or scale
Pause and resume: kubectl rollout pause deploy/app, then make several edits, then resume; restart pods with kubectl rollout restart deploy/app

revisionHistoryLimit (default 10) caps undoable revisions; use kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation to label history; Helm equivalent is helm rollback app <revision>, and in GitOps you git revert instead

Cheat sheet: maxUnavailable 0 + maxSurge 1 for zero downtime; always set readiness probes; Helm -f values-env.yaml then --set; --atomic for auto-rollback; Argo CD selfHeal + prune; canary via Rollouts steps + AnalysisTemplate
